subject: maths
title: Short Multiplication
seo_title: Year 4 Short Multiplication Worksheets: Grid Method and Formal Written Method
standard_text: Multiply two-digit and three-digit numbers by a one-digit number using formal written layout; solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law to multiply two digit numbers by one digit, integer scaling problems and harder correspondence problems such as n objects are connected to m objects.
meta_desc: Free Year 4 maths worksheets on short multiplication: partitioning and the grid method, 2-digit and 3-digit × 1-digit numbers with exchanging, scaling and correspondence problems, and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, following the National Curriculum.
key_big: Multiply the ones first. Exchange the tens and add them after you multiply the next column.
key_sub: 47 × 6: 7 × 6 = 42, write 2 and exchange 4. Then 4 × 6 = 24, add the 4 to make 28. Answer: 282. The grid method shows why: 40 × 6 + 7 × 6 = 240 + 42.
body_html:
Partition, multiply, add

A big multiplication is a few small ones. Partition the bigger number into tens and ones (or hundreds, tens and ones). Multiply each part. Then add the answers.

This is the same as 23 × 4 = 20 × 4 + 3 × 4. Remember that 20 × 4 is 2 tens × 4 = 8 tens = 80, not 8.

Short multiplication

Short multiplication is the formal written method. Write the numbers in columns with the ones lined up. Start with the ones. When an answer is 10 or more, write the ones digit and exchange the tens: write a small digit under the answer in the next column. Multiply first, then add the exchanged digit.

Short multiplication

47 × 6 = ?

Ones: 7 × 6 = 42. Write 2, exchange 4 tens. Tens: 4 × 6 = 24, then add the 4: 28. Write 28.

Answer: 282

Check with an estimate: 47 is close to 50, and 50 × 6 = 300. So 282 makes sense.

Times as many, and every one with every one

Scaling: “4 times as tall” means multiply by 4. A tower 4 times as tall as 23 cm is 23 × 4 = 92 cm.

Correspondence: 3 tops and 4 skirts. Each top goes with every skirt, so there are 3 × 4 = 12 outfits, not 3 + 4.

Multiply, then add: 3 packs of 24 stickers and 15 more is 3 × 24 + 15 = 72 + 15 = 87.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Forgetting the exchanged digit (23 × 4 = 82)Write the small digit under the next column and add it: 92
Adding the exchanged digit first (47 × 6 = 482)Multiply first: 4 × 6 = 24, then add 4: 28
Writing each answer side by side (23 × 4 = 812)12 ones = 1 ten and 2 ones. Write 2, exchange 1 ten: 8 tens + 1 ten = 9 tens
Treating 20 as 2 in the grid (20 × 4 = 8)20 × 4 = 2 tens × 4 = 8 tens = 80
Adding in a correspondence problem (3 tops, 4 skirts = 7)Each top goes with every skirt: 3 × 4 = 12

faq.a: It is the formal written method for multiplying by a one-digit number. You write the numbers in columns, multiply the ones first, and write any exchanged digit small in the next column so you can add it after multiplying.

faq.q: What is the grid method in maths?
faq.a: You partition the number into hundreds, tens and ones, write the parts across a grid and multiply each one. For 23 × 4 the grid shows 20 × 4 = 80 and 3 × 4 = 12, and 80 + 12 = 92.

faq.q: What times tables should a Year 4 child know?
faq.a: All of them up to 12 × 12. The National Curriculum expects children to recall multiplication and division facts for every table up to 12 × 12 by the end of Year 4.

faq.q: What is the Multiplication Tables Check?
faq.a: It is a short online check that Year 4 children in England take in June. There are 25 times tables questions up to 12 × 12, with 6 seconds to answer each one.

sets.title: Scaling, correspondence and multiplying then adding

items.q: A coach has 52 seats and a minibus has 16 seats. A school hires 1 coach and 3 minibuses. How many seats is that?
items.e: Minibuses: 3 × 16 = 48. Add the coach: 52 + 48 = 100.

items.q: Isla has 3 tops and 4 skirts. An outfit is one top and one skirt. How many different outfits can she make?
items.e: Each top goes with all 4 skirts: 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4 = 12 outfits. Adding (3 + 4) is a common mistake.

items.q: Ava has 46 stickers. Her brother has 3 times as many. How many stickers does her brother have?
items.e: “3 times as …” means multiply: 46 × 3. Ones: 6 × 3 = 18. Write 8, exchange 1 ten. Tens: 4 × 3 + 1 = 13. Write 13. Answer: 138. So the answer is 138.

items.q: A rabbit hutch is 75 cm long. The run in the garden is 3 times as long. How long is the run?
items.e: “3 times as …” means multiply: 75 cm × 3. Ones: 5 × 3 = 15. Write 5, exchange 1 ten. Tens: 7 × 3 + 1 = 22. Write 22. Answer: 225. So the answer is 225 cm.

items.q: Poppy buys 3 packs of 24 stickers. She already has 15 stickers. How many stickers does she have now?
items.e: Multiply first: 3 × 24 = 72. Then add: 72 + 15 = 87.

items.q: There are 2 paths from the school to the park and 5 paths from the park to the library. How many different ways can you walk from the school to the library through the park?
items.e: Each path to the park goes with all 5 paths on to the library: 5 + 5 = 2 × 5 = 10 ways. Adding (2 + 5) is a common mistake.

items.q: What number goes in the box? 14 × 7 + 6 × 7 = ☐ × 7
items.e: 14 lots of 7 and 6 lots of 7 make 20 lots of 7. So ☐ = 20. Check: 98 + 42 = 140 = 20 × 7.

items.q: A café sells 5 kinds of sandwich and 4 kinds of drink. A meal deal is one sandwich and one drink. How many different meal deals are there?
items.e: Each sandwich goes with all 4 drinks: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 5 × 4 = 20 meal deals. Adding (5 + 4) is a common mistake.

items.q: A jug holds 750 ml. A bucket holds 4 times as much. How much does the bucket hold?
items.e: “4 times as …” means multiply: 750 ml × 4. Ones: 0 × 4 = 0. Write 0. Tens: 5 × 4 = 20. Write 0, exchange 2 hundreds. Hundreds: 7 × 4 + 2 = 30. Write 30. Answer: 3,000. So the answer is 3,000 ml.

items.q: A school lunch menu has 4 main meals, 3 puddings and 2 drinks. Each child picks one main, one pudding and one drink. How many different lunches are there?
items.e: Main and pudding: 4 × 3 = 12. Each of those goes with 2 drinks: 12 × 2 = 24.

items.q: In the bike shed there are 7 bicycles and 4 tricycles. How many wheels are there altogether?
items.e: Bicycles: 7 × 2 = 14. Tricycles: 4 × 3 = 12. Add: 14 + 12 = 26.

items.q: An ice cream van has 6 flavours and 3 toppings. Each ice cream has one flavour and one topping. How many different ice creams can you choose?
items.e: Each flavour goes with all 3 toppings: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 6 × 3 = 18 ice creams. Adding (6 + 3) is a common mistake.

items.q: A small car has a mass of 925 kg. A lorry is 8 times as heavy. What is the mass of the lorry?
items.e: “8 times as …” means multiply: 925 kg × 8. Ones: 5 × 8 = 40. Write 0, exchange 4 tens. Tens: 2 × 8 + 4 = 20. Write 0, exchange 2 hundreds. Hundreds: 9 × 8 + 2 = 74. Write 74. Answer: 7,400. So the answer is 7,400 kg.

items.q: Jack plants 4 rows of 13 tulips. Then he plants 26 daffodils. How many flowers does he plant?
items.e: Tulips: 4 × 13 = 52. Add the daffodils: 52 + 26 = 78.

items.q: Alfie has some T-shirts and 3 pairs of shorts. He can make 15 different outfits of one T-shirt and one pair of shorts. How many T-shirts does he have?
items.e: Each T-shirt makes 3 outfits. ☐ × 3 = 15, and 5 × 3 = 15, so he has 5 T-shirts.

Which is the same as 23 × 4 + 23 × 2?
items.e: 4 lots of 23 and 2 more lots of 23 make 6 lots of 23: 23 × 4 + 23 × 2 = 23 × 6 = 138.

items.q: A school has 6 boxes of 144 pencils. It gives out 500 pencils. How many pencils are left?

items.q: A school books 4 coaches with 54 seats each. 187 people go on the trip. How many seats are empty?
